title: AI Risk Assessment
shortDefinition: A structured evaluation of a specific AI system's potential harms, failure modes, and risk level.
definition: An AI risk assessment is a structured evaluation of a specific AI system's potential harms, failure modes, and risk level — examining what could go wrong, how likely it is, how severe the consequences would be, and what safeguards are appropriate given that risk profile. Where AI governance establishes the overarching organizational policies and processes for managing AI risk, a risk assessment is the specific, applied evaluation conducted for an individual AI system or use case.

sections.title: What an AI risk assessment examines
sections.description: A thorough risk assessment evaluates consequence, likelihood, affected parties, and existing safeguards.

content.text: A thorough risk assessment evaluates several dimensions for a specific AI system: the consequence of a wrong or biased output (a misclassified email is low-stakes; a misclassified loan application is high-stakes), the likelihood of specific failure modes occurring given the system's design and training data, who could be harmed and how (specific affected groups, financial harm, safety harm, reputational harm), and what existing safeguards (guardrails, human review, explainability) already mitigate that risk versus what gaps remain. This produces a risk classification that informs how much additional governance, testing, or oversight the specific system needs.

items: Consequence severity — low-stakes vs. high-stakes outcomes.
Failure likelihood — probability of specific failure modes occurring.
Affected parties — who could be harmed and how.
Existing safeguards — guardrails, human review, explainability.
Risk classification — informs governance and oversight requirements.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: A risk assessment produces a risk classification that determines how much governance, testing, or oversight the specific system needs.

sections.title: AI risk assessment vs. AI governance: the relationship

content.text: AI governance is the organizational framework — policies, processes, accountability structures — for managing AI risk across your organization broadly. An AI risk assessment is the specific, applied exercise of evaluating an individual AI system against that framework, producing a risk classification and specific findings for that particular system. You typically need governance policies in place first (defining what risk levels mean and what's required at each level), then conduct risk assessments for each specific AI system to determine where it falls and what's required.

content.title: Complementary practices

sections.title: Limitations and risks of AI risk assessment

content.text: AI risk assessments have limitations. They are point-in-time evaluations — risks can emerge as systems evolve or usage patterns change. Assessments depend on available information — incomplete understanding of system behavior or training data limits assessment quality. Risk classification involves subjective judgment about likelihood and severity. Assessments can become outdated without periodic review, and over-reliance on assessment results without ongoing monitoring can create false confidence.

items: Point-in-time — risks can emerge after assessment.
Information dependence — incomplete data limits assessment quality.
Subjective judgment — likelihood and severity involve judgment.
Outdated risk — assessments need periodic review.
False confidence — assessment alone doesn't prevent risks.
Implementation gap — assessment findings must be acted upon.

content.title: Important
content.text: A risk assessment is a snapshot. Ongoing monitoring and periodic reassessment are essential for maintaining accurate risk awareness.

sections.title: Best practices for AI risk assessment

content.text: Conducting effective AI risk assessments requires structured methodology, stakeholder involvement, and actionable outputs. The following practices can help ensure your risk assessments deliver genuine risk management value.

content.title: Recommended approach:
items: Use established frameworks (NIST AI RMF) as a foundation.
Involve stakeholders who understand the system and its users.
Evaluate both consequence severity and likelihood.
Identify specific affected parties and potential harms.
Assess existing safeguards and their effectiveness.
Produce a clear risk classification and actionable recommendations.
Document assessment methodology and findings.
Plan for periodic reassessment after significant changes.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Measure remediation closure rate — risk assessments are only valuable when their findings are actually acted upon.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about AI risk assessment

items.question: Do we need a risk assessment for every AI system we use, even low-stakes ones?
items.answer: Assessment depth should scale with apparent risk — a brief assessment confirming a system is genuinely low-stakes is still valuable, while consequential systems warrant deeper evaluation.

items.question: What framework does ClickMasters use for risk assessment?
items.answer: ClickMasters draws on established frameworks like the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, adapted to your organization's specific context and risk tolerance.

items.question: Can a risk assessment be conducted on a system we're still developing, before launch?
items.answer: Yes, and this is often preferable — identifying risk issues before launch allows remediation to be built in rather than retrofitted after deployment.

items.question: How does a risk assessment differ from a bias audit?
items.answer: A bias audit specifically examines discriminatory outcomes across protected groups; a risk assessment is broader, examining the full range of potential harms and failure modes, of which bias is one specific category.

items.question: How long does an AI risk assessment take?
items.answer: 6–18 weeks depending on the number of systems assessed and whether ongoing methodology design is included.

items.question: Is a risk assessment a one-time exercise, or should it be repeated?
items.answer: Risk profiles can change as a system, its usage, or its underlying data evolves — periodic reassessment, particularly after significant changes, is a recommended practice.

items.question: What is the relationship between risk assessment and the EU AI Act?
items.answer: The EU AI Act requires risk classification of AI systems. A risk assessment provides the methodology and evidence for determining where a system falls within the Act's risk tiers (unacceptable, high, limited, minimal).

items.question: How do you assess likelihood in AI risk assessment?
items.answer: Likelihood assessment considers model performance, training data quality, deployment context, and known failure modes. ClickMasters uses a combination of quantitative metrics and expert judgment calibrated to your specific system.

items.question: What are the typical risk levels in AI risk assessment?
items.answer: Typical risk levels include low, medium, and high — corresponding to the severity of consequences and likelihood of occurrence. Each level triggers different governance requirements. ClickMasters uses a risk classification framework that maps to your organization's policies.

items.question: Can risk assessment help with vendor AI system evaluation?
items.answer: Yes — risk assessment methodology can be applied to third-party AI systems. This is increasingly important as organizations adopt AI tools and need to evaluate their risk profiles before deployment.
